overview:
In the context of Jainism and wider Indian temple architecture, the term "śikhara" (Sanskrit: शिखर) literally means "peak" or "summit" and refers to the superstructure that rises above the sanctum (garbhagṛha) of a temple. In Jain temples of the northern (Nāgara) architectural tradition, the śikhara is the most visually dominant element of the shrine, forming the vertical axis that marks the presence of the Jina and the sacred space below. The word itself evokes the image of a mountain peak, and this symbolism is central: the temple is conceived as a cosmic mountain, and the śikhara is its summit, where the devotee’s gaze and aspiration are directed upward toward liberation (mokṣa).

In Jain usage, the idea of a temple crowned by a śikhara is often expressed through the compound "śikharabaddha mandir"—a temple "bound" or "capped" with a peak. Such temples, whether dedicated to a particular Tīrthaṅkara or to multiple Jinas, feature one or more śikharas rising above the sanctum and sometimes above subsidiary shrines. The śikhara may be relatively simple and curvilinear (latina type) or elaborately clustered (śekharī or anekandaka type), with multiple miniature spires (ūrūśṛṅga) attached to the main tower. Jain temple cities such as Shatrunjaya (Palitana) and complexes like Kumbharia in Gujarat present skylines bristling with śikharas, visually expressing the multiplicity of shrines and the intensity of devotional and ascetic life.

Historically, Jain communities have negotiated the right to build śikharas in different political contexts. Under certain Islamic rulers, prominent temple superstructures were restricted, leading to flat-roofed shrines or concealed towers. The Digambara Jain Naya Mandir in Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi), completed in the early 19th century, is notable as the first Jain temple in that city to receive official permission for a śikhara under Mughal rule, marking a significant moment when Jain architectural expression could again publicly display its characteristic vertical emphasis. The presence or absence of a śikhara thus sometimes reflects not only theological symbolism but also historical conditions of patronage, tolerance, and negotiation.

From a symbolic perspective, the śikhara in Jain temples participates in a pan-Indian architectural language but is interpreted through Jain cosmology and ethics. The vertical ascent of the tower can be read as an architectural analogue of the soul’s journey from the lower realms of saṃsāra toward the upper regions of the Jain universe, culminating in Siddha-śilā, the realm of liberated beings. The temple’s plan and elevation, often aligned with vāstu and śilpa prescriptions, are understood as a disciplined ordering of space that supports right faith (samyag-darśana), right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), and right conduct (samyag-cāritra). In this way, the śikhara is not merely decorative; it is a visual and spatial aid to contemplation, reinforcing the Jain emphasis on inner ascent through non-violence, restraint, and meditation.

Architecturally, Jain śikharas share many features with Hindu Nāgara towers, including a square or stellate base, a curving outline that tapers toward the top, horizontal moldings, and a crowning element (āmalaka and kalasha in many traditions). Yet Jain patrons and craftsmen have developed distinctive idioms, especially in western India, where marble and finely carved sandstone are used to create dense sculptural programs on the śikhara surface. These may include images of Tīrthaṅkaras, yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs, narrative panels, and ornamental motifs, all integrated into the vertical rhythm of the tower. Over time, Jain temple architecture has also adapted to diasporic contexts, with modern śikharabaddha mandirs built outside India that retain the peak-like superstructure while accommodating contemporary materials and urban settings.

In Jain practice, the śikhara also functions as a marker of sacred presence in the landscape. Pilgrims approaching a tīrtha often first see the distant outline of śikharas rising above trees or hills, signaling the proximity of a place associated with the lives and liberations of Tīrthaṅkaras and other ascetics. On major pilgrimage hills such as Shatrunjaya and Girnar, the clustering of many śikharas on the slopes and summits reinforces the association between physical ascent and spiritual striving. While the core of Jain doctrine is preserved in canonical texts and philosophical treatises rather than architectural manuals, the śikhara has become one of the most recognizable visual expressions of Jain devotion, community identity, and the aspiration toward the highest spiritual peak.

primary_sources.title: Śilpa and Vāstu traditions on śikhara (representative verse)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous traditional śilpa-śāstra author (Hindu and Jain usage)
primary_sources.original_text: शिखरं पर्वताग्रं इव देवालयस्य शिरः स्मृतम् ।
primary_sources.transliteration: śikharaṃ parvatāgraṃ iva devālayasya śiraḥ smṛtam.
primary_sources.translation: The śikhara is remembered as the head of the temple, like the peak of a mountain.
primary_sources.notes: This representative formulation reflects the common Sanskrit understanding of śikhara as a mountain peak and the uppermost part of a temple superstructure. While individual śilpa-śāstra texts vary in wording, the metaphor of the temple as a mountain and the śikhara as its summit is consistent across Hindu and Jain architectural traditions. Jain temples following Nāgara architecture adopt this vocabulary, interpreting the mountain symbolism through Jain cosmology and the ascent toward liberation.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra (contextual cosmology for vertical symbolism)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.original_text: ऊर्ध्वं सिद्धाः अधो नरकाः मध्ये मनुष्यदेवाः ।
primary_sources.transliteration: ūrdhvaṃ siddhāḥ adho narakāḥ madhye manuṣya-devāḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Above are the liberated beings (siddhas), below are the hells, and in the middle are humans and gods.
primary_sources.notes: Although the Tattvārtha Sūtra does not discuss temple architecture or śikharas, this famous cosmological verse is often invoked to explain the vertical symbolism of Jain sacred spaces. The upward orientation of the śikhara is interpreted as an architectural reminder of the soul’s potential ascent to the realm of siddhas, aligning the physical form of the temple with doctrinal teachings about the structure of the universe and the goal of liberation.

primary_sources.title: Jain pilgrimage descriptions of Shatrunjaya and other temple cities
primary_sources.author: Various Jain authors in vernacular and Sanskrit/Prakrit
primary_sources.translation: On Mount Shatrunjaya, the multitude of temples crowned with many śikharas serves as a cause for people to remember the path to liberation.
primary_sources.notes: Pilgrimage manuals and praises of tīrthas often describe the skyline of Jain temple hills as filled with śikharas. While the exact wording differs across texts and languages, the idea that clustered śikharas visually evoke and reinforce remembrance of the mokṣa-mārga is widespread. This source type belongs to traditional devotional and descriptive literature (corpus tier D), linking architectural form with spiritual function in lived Jain practice.

misconceptions.myth: The śikhara is a purely decorative feature with no religious or symbolic significance in Jain temples.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain temple architecture, the śikhara is deeply symbolic. It represents the summit of a cosmic mountain and visually expresses the soul’s upward journey toward liberation. Its vertical emphasis, placement above the sanctum, and integration into pilgrimage landscapes all contribute to a theological reading of the temple as a structured aid to contemplation and spiritual ascent, not merely an ornamental tower.

misconceptions.myth: Only Hindu temples have śikharas; Jain temples use completely different architectural forms.
misconceptions.reality: Jain temples in the Nāgara tradition share the śikhara superstructure with Hindu temples, drawing on common śilpa and vāstu canons. However, Jain patrons and artisans adapt this form to Jain iconography, cosmology, and ritual needs. Temple cities such as Shatrunjaya, Kumbharia, and many modern śikharabaddha mandirs clearly show Jain usage of śikharas, often with distinctive marble carving, Tīrthaṅkara imagery, and layouts tailored to Jain pilgrimage and worship.

misconceptions.myth: If a Jain temple lacks a visible śikhara, it is necessarily less orthodox or less sacred.
misconceptions.reality: The presence or absence of a visible śikhara can reflect historical, political, or practical constraints rather than doctrinal inferiority. In some periods and regions, rulers restricted prominent temple towers, leading Jain communities to build flat-roofed shrines or more modest superstructures. Such temples remain fully valid places of worship, and their sanctity depends on the consecrated images, rituals, and adherence to Jain ethical and spiritual principles, not solely on architectural height.
